title: How tea conquered Britain
paragraphs: Tea is so closely associated with Britain today that it is easy to forget it was once an exotic luxury. The drink first arrived in London in the 1650s, brought by Dutch traders, and was sold in coffee houses as a medicine. Advertisements of the time claimed that it could cure headaches, aid digestion and even prevent bad dreams. At around ten times the price of coffee, however, it was beyond the reach of most people.

Its rise in popularity owed much to a royal marriage. In 1662 King Charles II married the Portuguese princess Catherine of Braganza, who had grown up drinking tea and brought the habit to court. Where the queen led, the wealthy followed. Tea drinking became a sign of refinement, and an entire industry grew up around it, producing fine porcelain cups, silver teapots and locked wooden boxes called caddies, in which the precious leaves were kept away from servants.

Throughout the eighteenth century, the government taxed tea heavily, at times at more than a hundred per cent of its value. The result was a thriving illegal trade. Smugglers brought tea in from continental Europe and landed it secretly on the south coast, and it has been estimated that by the 1770s more tea entered Britain illegally than legally. Some smuggled tea was mixed with other leaves, or even sheep dung, to make it go further. In 1784 the government finally cut the tax from 119 per cent to just over 12 per cent, and smuggling almost disappeared within a few years.

Cheaper tea transformed the national diet. By the early nineteenth century it was drunk by every class, and for poor families it often replaced beer as the main drink. Some historians argue that this was good for public health, because water had to be boiled to make tea, killing many of the organisms that caused disease. Others point out that tea had little nutritional value, and that families who spent money on tea and sugar sometimes went without more nourishing food.

For most of this period, almost all of Britain's tea came from China, which would only accept silver in payment. To reduce this dependence, the British East India Company began growing tea in India in the 1830s. A botanist, Robert Fortune, was sent to China in disguise to collect plants and seeds and to learn the secrets of tea processing. Although many of the Chinese plants he smuggled out did poorly, a variety native to Assam in north-east India thrived, and by the end of the century India had overtaken China as Britain's main supplier.

The twentieth century brought further change. The tea bag, which was first sold in the United States, was slow to catch on in Britain, accounting for only about three per cent of the market in 1968. Within thirty years, however, it was used for almost all the tea made in British homes. Today tea faces competition from coffee, particularly among younger people, yet Britons still drink roughly a hundred million cups of it every day.

title: Trees in the city
paragraphs: For much of the twentieth century, city planners saw street trees mainly as decoration. They were planted to make streets look pleasant, and cut down without much thought when roads were widened or pipes needed repairing. Over the past three decades, however, a growing body of research has changed that view. Trees are now increasingly treated as infrastructure, as essential to a city's functioning as its drains or its bus routes.

The most obvious benefit is cooling. A mature tree can lower the temperature of the air around it by several degrees, partly by providing shade and partly through transpiration, the release of water vapour from its leaves. Studies in several cities have found that streets with dense tree cover can be up to five degrees cooler on summer afternoons than similar streets without trees. As heatwaves become more frequent, this effect is becoming a matter of public health.

Trees also help manage water. In a heavy storm, rain falling on roads and roofs runs straight into the drains, which can become overwhelmed and cause flooding. Tree canopies intercept a proportion of the rain before it reaches the ground, and their roots help water soak into the soil. A study in one American city estimated that its trees prevented hundreds of millions of litres of water from entering the drains each year, saving the city the cost of building larger pipes.

The benefits to people are harder to measure but may be just as important. Hospital patients with a view of trees have been found to recover faster and need fewer painkillers than those facing a brick wall. In residential areas, more trees have been linked with lower levels of stress and, in some studies, with lower crime, although researchers are cautious about whether trees themselves are responsible or simply tend to be found in wealthier neighbourhoods.

That last point highlights a problem of fairness. In many cities, tree cover is far higher in wealthy districts than in poor ones, which means the people least able to afford air conditioning are often the most exposed to heat. Some cities have begun mapping tree cover street by street and prioritising planting in the areas with the fewest trees. Others have set targets for the proportion of the city covered by tree canopy, such as thirty per cent by 2040.

Planting trees is not enough on its own, however. Urban trees face difficult conditions: compacted soil, limited space for roots, pollution and damage from vehicles. Many young trees die within a few years of planting, often because they are not watered during their first summers. Experts therefore argue that money for maintenance matters as much as money for planting, and that choosing the right species for each location, including species that can cope with a hotter climate, is essential.

title: Why we laugh
paragraphs: Ask people why they laugh and most will say it is because something is funny. Yet when researchers have recorded people laughing in everyday situations, they have found that only a small proportion of laughter follows anything resembling a joke. Most laughter occurs after ordinary remarks such as 'See you later' or 'I know what you mean'. This suggests that laughter is less about humour than about relationships.

Further evidence comes from the fact that we laugh far more in company than alone. One study asked participants to keep a diary of every time they laughed, and found they were around thirty times more likely to laugh when other people were present. Even when watching a comedy, people laugh more if they are watching with friends. Laughter, it seems, is a signal sent to others, telling them that we are relaxed, that we feel friendly towards them, and that the situation is safe.

Laughter is not unique to humans. Chimpanzees, gorillas and other great apes produce a breathy panting sound during play, particularly when they are tickled, and this is widely thought to be an early form of laughter. Rats, too, produce high-pitched calls when tickled, too high for humans to hear without special equipment. Such findings suggest that laughter evolved long before language, as a way of showing that rough play was not a real attack.

One reason laughter may be so effective at bringing people together is its effect on the body. Laughing releases chemicals in the brain called endorphins, which produce feelings of pleasure and reduce pain. In one experiment, people who had watched a comedy video were able to tolerate more discomfort than those who had watched a documentary. The researchers suggest that the endorphin effect helps explain why shared laughter makes people feel closer.

Laughter is also highly contagious. Hearing someone laugh activates areas of the brain that prepare the face for smiling, which is why television comedies have long used recorded laughter. The effect can sometimes spread on a large scale. In 1962, in a school in what is now Tanzania, a fit of laughter spread from a few pupils to hundreds of people across several villages, and schools were closed for months.

Not all laughter is the same, however. Listeners can usually tell the difference between spontaneous laughter and laughter that is produced deliberately, for example out of politeness. Spontaneous laughter tends to be higher in pitch and contains sounds that would be difficult to make on purpose. Interestingly, the ability to tell the two apart appears to improve with age, perhaps because adults have more experience of social situations in which polite laughter is used.

title: The desert locust
paragraphs: For most of its life, the desert locust is an unremarkable insect. It lives alone in the dry regions stretching from West Africa to India, feeding on scattered plants and avoiding others of its kind. In this solitary phase it is green or brown and does little damage. Yet under certain conditions the same species can transform into one of the most destructive pests on Earth, forming swarms that can contain billions of insects.

The transformation begins with rain. After unusually heavy rainfall in the desert, plants grow quickly, and locusts breed rapidly. When the plants later begin to dry out, the insects are forced together into the remaining green areas. Crowding is the key trigger. Experiments have shown that when locusts are repeatedly touched on their back legs by other locusts, they begin to change both their behaviour and their appearance within a few hours.

The crowded, or gregarious, locusts become attracted to one another rather than avoiding contact. Over several generations they also change colour, becoming bright yellow and black, and develop stronger flight muscles. Young locusts that cannot yet fly form marching bands on the ground, and once they become adults, they take to the air together. A single swarm can travel over a hundred kilometres in a day, carried by the wind.

The damage swarms cause is enormous. An adult locust can eat roughly its own weight in fresh food every day, and a swarm covering one square kilometre can eat as much in a day as tens of thousands of people. Because swarms can cross national borders, an outbreak in one country can quickly become a problem for several others. Major plagues have affected the food supply of millions of people, most recently between 2019 and 2021 in East Africa.

For many years, the main method of control was to spray swarms with chemical insecticides from aircraft or vehicles. This can be effective, but the chemicals can harm other wildlife and people, and swarms are often in remote areas that are difficult to reach. Increasingly, the emphasis has shifted towards prevention. Organisations monitor rainfall and vegetation using satellite images, and teams on the ground check areas where breeding is likely, so that small groups can be treated before they form swarms.

Researchers are also developing gentler methods. One is a natural fungus that infects locusts but is harmless to most other animals; it works more slowly than chemicals but leaves no toxic residue. Another approach makes use of the chemical signals locusts use to communicate, with the aim of disrupting the crowding process itself. Scientists warn, however, that climate change may make heavy rainfall in desert regions more common, which could increase the risk of future plagues.

title: The rise of remote work
paragraphs: Working from home is not a new idea. In the 1970s, an American engineer named Jack Nilles coined the term telecommuting and predicted that computers would allow many office workers to avoid the daily journey. For decades, however, his prediction came true only slowly. Most employers remained convinced that staff needed to be seen in order to work hard, and the technology for working together at a distance was limited.

The situation changed abruptly in 2020, when lockdowns forced millions of office workers to work from home almost overnight. Surveys in several countries found that the proportion of people working mainly from home rose from a few per cent to more than a third within weeks. Video calls, shared documents and messaging tools, which had existed for years, suddenly became part of everyday working life.

Many workers discovered advantages they had not expected. The most commonly mentioned was the time saved by not commuting, which for some amounted to more than an hour a day. Others valued the flexibility to fit work around family responsibilities, or the ability to concentrate without the interruptions of an open-plan office. Some studies found that productivity was maintained or even improved, particularly for tasks that required focused individual work.

There were drawbacks too. Junior employees, in particular, reported that they found it harder to learn from more experienced colleagues when they could not observe them at work or ask quick questions. Many people found it difficult to separate work from home life, and reported working longer hours. Feelings of isolation were common, especially among those who lived alone. Managers worried that creativity and informal problem-solving, which often happen in chance conversations, would suffer.

As restrictions ended, many organisations settled on a compromise known as hybrid working, in which employees spend some days in the office and some at home. The office itself has begun to change as a result. Rather than rows of individual desks, some companies are creating spaces designed for meetings and collaboration, on the grounds that individual work can be done at home. Others have reduced the size of their offices to save on rent.

The long-term effects are still uncertain. City centres that depended on office workers have seen fewer customers in cafés and shops, while some suburbs and smaller towns have benefited. Some economists believe remote work could allow people to live further from expensive cities, reducing housing pressure, while others warn that jobs that can be done from anywhere might eventually be moved to countries where wages are lower.

title: Navigating the Pacific
paragraphs: The islands of the Pacific Ocean are scattered across an area larger than all of the world's land put together, and some lie thousands of kilometres from their nearest neighbour. Yet by around 1250 CE, people had settled almost every habitable island in this vast region, from Hawaii in the north to New Zealand in the south. They did so in wooden sailing canoes, without metal tools, compasses or maps. How they achieved this has long fascinated scholars.

For a time, some Western researchers doubted that such voyages could have been deliberate. In the 1950s, one influential writer argued that the islands must have been settled by accident, by canoes blown off course by storms. This view was challenged by later studies, which used computer simulations of winds and currents. They showed that drifting canoes would almost never have reached the most remote islands, such as Hawaii, and that settlement must have involved intentional navigation.

Traditional navigators relied on a detailed knowledge of the natural world. At night, they steered by the points on the horizon where particular stars rose and set, memorising sequences of stars for each route. By day, they used the sun and, crucially, the patterns of ocean swells, the long waves created by distant winds. An experienced navigator could feel the direction of several swells through the movement of the canoe, even with closed eyes.

Finding an island also depended on signs that land was near. Certain seabirds fly out to sea to feed in the morning and return to land in the evening, so following them at dusk could lead a canoe towards an island. Clouds tend to gather over islands, and in some lagoons the light reflected from shallow water gives clouds a greenish tint. Navigators also noticed how islands disturbed the pattern of swells, creating changes that could be detected long before land was visible.

Much of this knowledge was nearly lost. Colonial authorities and missionaries discouraged traditional voyaging, and by the mid-twentieth century only a few navigators remained, mostly on small islands in Micronesia. One of them, Mau Piailug, agreed in 1976 to guide a reconstructed double canoe called Hokule'a from Hawaii to Tahiti, a distance of more than four thousand kilometres, using only traditional methods. The voyage succeeded and attracted wide attention.

The voyage of Hokule'a sparked a revival. Piailug went on to train a new generation of navigators, including people from islands where the knowledge had disappeared. Today, voyaging societies across the Pacific build canoes and teach traditional navigation, and the canoe has become a symbol of cultural pride. The revival has also contributed to scholarship, as modern voyages have tested ideas about how the original settlement took place.
